scenes.title: Airflow Deferrable Operators
scenes.narration: This lesson explains deferrable operators, the Airflow feature that lets tasks wait efficiently without hogging worker resources.

scenes.title: The cost of naive waiting
bullets: Classic sensors occupy a worker slot while waiting
A long-running poll can block real work
Many waiters can starve the whole cluster
scenes.narration: The problem deferrable operators address is the cost of waiting. A classic sensor, even one just polling for a file, occupies a full worker slot the entire time it waits. When a task waits for hours, that slot is wasted, and if many tasks are waiting at once they can starve the cluster of the capacity needed to do real work.

scenes.title: How deferral works
steps: Task starts and hits an async wait
It defers, releasing its worker slot
Task resumes on a worker when ready
scenes.narration: A deferrable operator solves this by handing off its wait. When the task reaches a point where it must wait, it defers, releasing its worker slot entirely. A lightweight component called a trigger, running in the async triggerer process, watches the condition on the task's behalf. Only once the condition is met does the task resume on a worker to finish. So the expensive worker slot is occupied for compute, never for idle waiting.

scenes.title: The triggerer and asyncio
bullets: A dedicated triggerer process runs triggers
Triggers are async, built on asyncio
One triggerer handles thousands of waits cheaply
scenes.narration: Deferral relies on a dedicated triggerer process that must be running in your deployment. Triggers are asynchronous coroutines built on Python's asyncio, which is what lets a single triggerer efficiently monitor thousands of pending conditions at once, far more scalably than tying up a worker per wait.

scenes.title: Using a deferrable operator
scenes.code:
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor

wait_for_file = S3KeySensor(
    task_id='wait_for_file',
    bucket_name='my-bucket',
    bucket_key='data/{{ ds }}/ready.flag',
    deferrable=True,
)
scenes.narration: Many modern operators expose deferral through a simple flag. Here an S3 key sensor waits for a daily ready-flag file, and setting deferrable to true means that instead of polling on a worker, it defers to the triggerer. The templated date in the key path makes it wait for the correct partition each run. Enabling deferral is often this easy, yet it can dramatically cut resource usage on wait-heavy pipelines.

scenes.text: Enable deferrable=True on long waits and run a triggerer, so waiting tasks cost almost nothing and workers stay free for real compute.
scenes.narration: The best practice is to enable deferral on any long-waiting task and ensure a triggerer is running, so that waiting costs almost nothing and your workers stay free to perform the real computation your pipelines need.
